HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, descriptive — answering "How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?"):

Among Black respondents in the NLSY79 data, incarceration is associated with a near-complete stall — and for those who started with some wealth, an outright reversal — of wealth accumulation, and the setback scales with initial socioeconomic position. Stratifying Black respondents (n=3,013; 159 ever jailed) by terciles of 1985 baseline wealth as a proxy for income level: in the lowest tercile (1985 median wealth ≈ $0), jailed respondents remain pinned at $0 median wealth through 1996, capturing only ~30% of the wealth growth their non-jailed peers achieve ($6,077 vs $20,203 mean change, winsorized). In the middle tercile, jailed respondents' median wealth change by 1996 is negative (−$1,000) versus +$6,231 for non-jailed peers; in the highest tercile it is strongly negative (−$5,800) versus +$8,825, meaning jailed respondents in the top tercile end 1996 with less wealth than they had in 1985. The absolute wealth gap between ever-jailed and never-jailed Black respondents widens monotonically with initial wealth: ≈$14K (low), ≈$28K (mid), ≈$52K (high) in winsorized mean 1985→1996 change, and an OLS on winsorized 1996 change with a jailed×tercile interaction (controlling sex) confirms the penalty is significantly more negative in the top tercile (interaction −$35.2K, p=0.017). Thus, contrary to the intuition that the poor are hit hardest, the dollar and proportional wealth setback from incarceration is largest for Black individuals who started with mid-to-high wealth, while for the poorest third incarceration is associated with being locked out of wealth accumulation entirely (median wealth stuck at $0). All comparisons are descriptive associations, not causal effects: the jailed group already had less wealth in 1985, the treatment window (1985–1994) overlaps the 1985→1990 change, and the composite wealth measure is coarse (many exact zeros/negatives).

Brief race context (optional, as agreed): the pattern of jailed respondents' median 1996 wealth collapsing to $0 holds for all races (white: $9,000 vs $0; hispanic: $17,075 vs $0), but incarceration rates are far higher among Black men (9.8%) than white (1.6%) or hispanic (5.7%) men, so the racial incidence of the exposure differs even if the within-group wealth pattern is similar.

payload.workflow: 1) Inspected data (12,013×6, no missing; race categories white/black/'hipanic'). 2) Restricted to Black respondents (n=3,013). 3) Stratified by terciles of 1985 composite wealth (pre-treatment baseline, proxy for income level). 4) Computed wealth changes 1985→1990 and 1985→1996 by ever_jailed within each tercile; reported cell sizes, medians, and 1%/99% winsorized means. 5) 1996 treated as main post-treatment contrast; 1990 as intermediate point (window 1985–1994 may still be active). 6) OLS on winsorized change with jailed×tercile interaction and sex control. 7) Brief race context comparison (optional). Script: analysis_nls_incarceration.py.
